title: Conditions for scale
lede: A good school model still needs a system that lets it open, measure itself and be judged fairly. Three conditions decide that: whether accountability tells anyone which schools are working, whether the data infrastructure to answer that question still exists, and whether capital is flowing toward new schools. All three moved in 2025 and 2026, mostly in the direction of less measurement.

items.headline: The decline predates the pandemic and tracks the rollback.
items.detail: The Education Scorecard dates the learning recession to 2013 and notes it coincided with the dismantling of test-based accountability and the rise of social media, without claiming to have separated the two. For an investor in school models, this is the argument that measurement itself is part of the intervention.

items.headline: School ratings already hide the students they were built to surface.
items.detail: Thirty states set the minimum group size for reporting at 20 or higher and only 13 use 10, so a school can be rated well while a small group of students inside it is not counted at all.

items.headline: Federal flexibility is expanding, not contracting.
items.detail: Eight states now hold ESEA waivers under the Department's Returning Education to the States initiative, Ohio the latest on October 30, 2026. Most are about money, consolidating federal funding streams, but two reach accountability: Indiana no longer has to give academic indicators much greater weight in high school ratings, and Arkansas may count advanced students' high school test results in place of grade-level tests. More state variation follows, which makes cross-state comparison of a model's results harder precisely as networks try to expand across state lines.

items.headline: There is a live question about whether any of it works.
items.detail: Assessment researchers are now asking whether accountability systems identify the right schools, whether anyone uses the results, and whether identified schools actually improve. New Hampshire found its identified schools improved faster than matched controls; most states have not checked.

items.label: Students in the national achievement database
items.note: The Stanford Education Data Archive links state tests to a common scale. It is the only way to compare a model's results across state lines, and it is grant-funded rather than statutory.

items.label: Districts improving faster than matched peers
items.note: A ready-made sourcing list: districts that gained at least 0.3 grade levels in both reading and math against peers of similar size, poverty and demographics in their own state.

items.label: The federal evidence clearinghouse
items.note: The What Works Clearinghouse remains the federal evidence review, inside an agency publishing a restructuring strategy and now funded by a continuing resolution that expires December 11, 2026. Evidence for ESSA at Johns Hopkins is the independent alternative.

items.label: Program ratings in the independent catalog
items.note: Across reading, math, attendance and family engagement. Whole-school models are a thin slice of it: most rated entries are programs that run inside a school, not designs for the school itself.

blocks.subtitle: Announced commitments and the vehicles behind them. Amounts are as announced by the funder; deployment schedules are rarely published.

The field's main engine for turning promising interventions into rated evidence, and a natural co-funder for any model that needs an evaluation partner

A federal credit of up to $1,700 per taxpayer for contributions to approved scholarship-granting organizations, starting January 1, 2027. Thirty states had filed an advance election to participate as of September 14, 2026, under Revenue Procedure 2026-6

Demand-side capital at a scale no philanthropy can match, routed to tuition at private schools and microschools rather than to new public-school buildings. It changes who a new public school competes with for students, not how many public seats exist

Eight new state-entity grants worth $416.1 million in total expected funding, awarded September 8, 2026 through the Department of Labor: Texas Education Agency $149.2M, The Mind Trust $68.9M, Florida $53.9M, South Carolina $48.2M, Michigan $38.6M, Excellent Schools Washington $33.3M, Delaware $16.0M, North Dakota $8.0M

Federal start-up and replication money is at a high and concentrated in a few states, Texas above all. For a funder, it lowers the cost of opening in those states and raises the premium on knowing which of the new schools work

items.headline: Whether the charter effect is real.
items.detail: CREDO reports positive average effects; the National Education Policy Center argues they fall below what researchers treat as meaningful and that the days-of-learning conversion inflates them. Both readings are defensible from the same numbers, which is why the sector average is a poor basis for an investment.

items.headline: Whether AI-first schools are a model or a marketing claim.
items.detail: Operators publish top-percentile results on external instruments; researchers point out there is no comparison group, the population is self-selected and tuition-paying, and that a 2025 review found intelligent tutoring barely beats non-AI tutoring built on the same active-learning principles. October moved the argument without settling it: the New York Times reported that only 42% of Alpha students met the company's own '2x' growth standard in both subjects. It is a reporter's reading of operator data, not an evaluation, and no public-school pilot yet runs the full model against a comparison group.

items.headline: How many microschool students exist.
items.detail: Estimates run from 750,000 to 2 million depending on definition, and most microschools sit outside state assessment entirely. The Center's own 2026 survey reports that operators now rank growth in nonacademic learning as their most desired student outcome, so the measurement gap is becoming a design choice rather than a growing pain. A sector that cannot be counted cannot be evaluated, which is an argument for funding measurement before models.

items.headline: Whether tutoring's effects survive scale.
items.detail: High-dosage tutoring produces some of the largest effects in education research, and those effects shrink as programs grow. Saga's own studies range from +0.09 to +0.19 SD depending on the site and year.

items.headline: Whether an AI tutor adds learning or displaces it.
items.detail: The two best-powered randomized trials point opposite ways. In 18 Tennessee middle schools, Khanmigo produced roughly 0.06 to 0.08 SD a year, similar to Khan practice without the AI. In a trial of 2,379 undergraduates at a large U.S. public university, access to a course-integrated AI tutor cut final grades by 0.37 SD and engagement with existing coursework by 0.90 SD, with larger losses for first-generation students. The populations and settings differ and neither settles the K-12 question. But the mechanism the second proposes, displacement rather than augmentation, is the one an AI-first school design most needs to rule out, and nobody has yet.
